summary:
Eskişehir stands under the national framework applicable in Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than residual prejudice. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' prison through an amendment to the indecent-acts provision. The same package would impose sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care, including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements, and could expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges, all justified as protecting "the family and public morals".

Eskişehir itself has a documented record of suppression. In June 2021 police blocked the city's first Pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have moved against the local Pride event. Duvar English reported that officers reached the assembly area hours before the scheduled start time and carried out identity checks; organisers were not permitted to hold a press conference or conduct the march, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of "violating the ban on the march". The intervention followed similar police action against Pride events in Istanbul and Ankara days earlier. Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years, citing security concerns and public order.

On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex", a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. Kadir Has University surveys recorded public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

The June 2021 police blockade of Eskişehir's first Pride march occurred days after comparable interventions in Istanbul and Ankara, indicating coordinated national practice rather than an isolated local decision. Turkish authorities' stated grounds for banning Pride events in recent years have been security concerns and public order.

Public opinion data from Kadir Has University shows support for equal LGBTQ rights rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020, a shift that has not been matched by legal reform; ILGA-Europe's 2026 ranking placed Turkey 47th of 49 countries.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch in October 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources. Early 2026 reporting indicated the specific provision criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" was not included in that year's judicial reform package, but the status of the wider package's other provisions, including the gender-affirming care restrictions, is not stated.

The sources do not document any Eskişehir-specific enforcement against trans individuals beyond the June 2021 Pride intervention; local policing practice toward trans residents and visitors in Eskişehir is not sourced.
